field_proj_summary: In 2000, Congress approved and funded a 30-year restoration effort for the Florida Everglades­­––the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan (CERP). In 2008, the National Academies of Sciences recommended that restoration projects in the Everglades include the long-term effects of environmental change, including sea level rise. Because CERP involves federal, state, and local partnerships, along with guaranteed funding, it serves as a platform from which to effectively plan and implement adaptation.

title: Atuliqtuq: A Collaborative Approach in Support of the Nunavut Climate Change Adaptation Plan
field_citation: Hitt, J. &amp; Gregg, R.M. (2010). Atuliqtuq: A Collaborative Approach in Support of the Nunavut Climate Change Adaptation Plan [Case study on a project of the Canadian Institute of Planners, Government of Nunavut, Natural Resources Canada, and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development]. Product of EcoAdapt&#39;s State of Adaptation Program. Retrieved from CAKE: http://www.cakex.org/case-studies/atuliqtuq-collaborative-approach-support-nunavut-climate-change-adaptation-plan (Last updated December 2010)
field_photo_credit: Photo attributed to Ansgar Walk. Incorporated here under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.5 Generic license. No endorsement by licensor implied.
field_proj_background: Residents of Nunavut have observed alarming changes in their environment. Decreasing levels of permafrost and sea ice, rising sea levels, and severe coastal erosion have caused local Nunavut communities to fear for the safety and sustainability of their communities.In 2003, the Government of Nunavut created a strategy to prepare the territory for climate change and increase the local community&rsquo;s resilience and adaptive capacity.&nbsp; Two key priorities of the Nunavut Climate Change Strategy called for increasing climate change knowledge and building the capacity of the territory and its local governments to take adaptation action. To help achieve these goals, the Government of Nunavut joined together with the CIP, DIAND, and NRCan to form a multiyear project, the Nunavut Climate Change Partnership. The primary objective of this partnership is to increase the capacity of Nunavut communities to begin planning and implementing effective adaptation at a local level.
field_proj_implement: The partnership&rsquo;s effort is often referred to as Atuliqtuq or &lsquo;coming into force&rsquo; in Inuktitut. Atuliqtuq perfectly describes the partnership&rsquo;s goals as they worked together to bring each organization&rsquo;s expertise and resources together to safeguard the local communities of Nunavut and their cultures.&nbsp;The multi-year project engages local institutions such as the Ittaq Heritage and Research Centre in Clyde River and the Nunavut Research Institute in Iqaluit to ensure that the information collected includes Inuit Quajimajatuqangit, or traditional environmental knowledge (TEK), and that the policy solutions defined by the process would be in the spirit of the culture of the area.The Nunavut Climate Change Partnership continues to work to increase the local and regional resilience and capacity focusing on three initiatives: building capacity, increasing local scientific knowledge, and developing tools to support local adaptation action.Building Capacity:The partnership will develop pilot local adaptation projects in seven Nunavut communities - Clyde River, Hall Beach, Iqaluit, Arviat, Whale Cove, Cambridge Bay, and Kugluktuk - using the data collected by the partnership to act as models for future regional climate change adaptation action.Increasing scientific knowledge:Nunavut Permafrost Monitoring Network: Permafrost monitoring sites were established in six Nunavut communities in the Baffin Region (Resolute, Igoolik, Arctic Bay, Pond Inlet, Clyde River, and Pangnirtung) to establish local baseline data, contribute to the national permafrost monitoring network, and support local climate change adaptation planning.Arctic sea level rise and coastal hazards assessment: The assessment looked at the impact local and regional sea level rise and resulting coastal hazards such as coastal erosion would have on coastal communities.Regional drinking water analysis: An analysis of a few Nunavut communities&rsquo; continued access to freshwater supplies in the face of climate change.TEK: The CIP led an effort to collect Inuit TEK, which will also be used in developing local adaptation plans.The scientific support for the studies conducted was provided by NRCan and the sea level rise and coastal hazards assessment as well as the water analysis will serve as models for other future regional assessments in other territories and provinces.Developing adaptation support tools:The CIP is developing a Community Climate Change Adaptation Toolkit, which will incorporate existing scientific information, data collected by the partnership, and best practices from community adaptation action plans into a set of guidelines Nunavut communities will be able to use to produce their own adaptation plans.
field_proj_outcomes: The information, tools, and community case studies created by the Nunavut Climate Change Partnership will be used to develop and create the Nunavut Climate Change Adaptation Strategy. The data and case studies will also be used as models by other Nunavut communities as well as other coastal communities around the region.
field_proj_status: Information was collected from online resources. Updated 12/21/10
field_proj_summary: To increase provincial and local ability to adapt to climate change, the Government of Nunavut joined together with the Canadian Institute of Planners (CIP), Natural Resources Canada (NRCan), and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (DIAND) to form a partnership to support local communities while helping to develop Nunavut&rsquo;s climate change adaptation strategy. The partnership&rsquo;s effort, often called Atuliqtuq (&lsquo;coming into force&rsquo;), developed projects to increase understanding of how climate impacts will affect the region and develop case studies for other communities to follow.

title: Nunavut Climate Change Strategy
field_citation: Hitt, J. (2010). Nunavut Climate Change Strategy [Case study on a project of the Nunavut Department of Environment]. Product of EcoAdapt&#39;s State of Adaptation Program. Retrieved from CAKE: http://www.cakex.org/case-studies/nunavut-climate-change-strategy (Last updated December 2010)
field_photo_credit: Photo attributed to Susanna Haas. Incorporated here under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 2.0 Generic license. No endorsement by licensor implied.
field_proj_background: Local observations and traditional knowledge from indigenous communities around the territory of Nunavut are demonstrating that the region is already experiencing a number of climate change impacts. Communities are experiencing dramatic sea ice loss, shifting habitats for the territory&rsquo;s most iconic species, and increasing temperatures. These impacts are having a huge effect on the territory&rsquo;s economy and culture, particularly the region&rsquo;s indigenous culture. To prepare the territory for the impacts of climate change, the Government of Nunavut identified three key priorities to make the region more resilient: increasing the climate change knowledge of the province, building the capacity for adaptation action, and reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
field_proj_implement: The Nunavut Climate Change Strategy, created by the Department of the Environment, creates a framework for action and outlines measures and goals, but is not an implementation plan. The strategy outlines goals to be achieved during a ten-year timeframe ending in 2013. The strategy mandates the Department of the Environment to enact a monitoring plan to track the impacts of climate change on the territory and develop strategies and materials to communicate those impacts. The strategy also outlines extensive outreach objectives for the territory aiming to increase awareness. To advance knowledge of impacts and possible adaptation strategies, the strategy calls for Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit, or sharing of Inuit traditional knowledge, and Pillimmaksaniq, or community involvement.&nbsp;
field_proj_outcomes: The strategy developed by the Government of Nunavut was an extremely helpful and informative process for the region. It helped outline priorities for the government and public and spurred a number of local community adaptation projects.
field_proj_status: Information collected from online resources. Updated 12/21/10
field_proj_summary: Nunavut has already experienced a number of climate change impacts, including loss of sea ice, permafrost, and habitat for key species. The Nunavut Department of the Environment developed a climate change strategy to address and prepare the province for future climate change.

title: Creating a More Resilient Yellowknife: Climate Change Impacts and Municipal Decision Making
field_citation: Hitt, J. (2010). Creating a More Resilient Yellowknife: Climate Change Impacts and Municipal Decision Making [Case study on a project of the City of Yellowknife]. Product of EcoAdapt&#39;s State of Adaptation Program. Retrieved from CAKE: http://www.cakex.org/case-studies/creating-more-resilient-yellowknife-climate-change-impacts-and-municipal-decision (Last updated December 2010)
field_photo_credit: Photo attributed to Trevor MacInnis. This work has been released into the public domain by its author. No endorsement by licensor implied.
field_proj_background: Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, located near the Arctic Circle, has experienced noticeable changes in the surrounding environment over the past decade. As the weather warms, residents and hunters are seeing species that have previously never ventured as far north, such as the white deer, crows, and cougars. The city has also experienced infrastructure problems such as buckling roadways with changing permafrost layers, and problems with the city&rsquo;s drinking water as the surrounding rivers have higher turbidity levels than normal due to increased erosion. The city has sought to deal with climate change impacts on a case-by-case basis, typically giving band-aid solutions to a larger, more serious problem.The adaptation planning process aimed to bring together relevant stakeholders to incorporate future conditions into management and planning policies and increase citywide collaboration on addressing climate change impacts.
field_proj_implement: In 2007, the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs awarded the City of Yellowknife a $70,000 grant to be used for adaptation planning. The planning process involved city council and staff, the Government of the Northwest Territories, and outside partners at Ecology North and Dene Nations; the process was facilitated by the Pembina Institute. The project targeted elected officials and city administrators in order to inform them about the impacts of climate change and arm Yellowknife with the information, capacity, and tools needed to make the city more resilient to climate change.Three half-day workshops were hosted for decision makers. The workshops focused on creating a common understanding of climate change adaptation, identifying observed climate impacts, and exploring opportunities for adaptation implementation. Participants were led through a process that reviewed historical and future climate scenarios for the region, introduced case studies from other jurisdictions experiencing similar impacts, and identified where and how climate change impacts and information can be integrated into the city&rsquo;s management, policies, zoning, and practices to increase Yellowknife&rsquo;s resilience.
field_proj_outcomes: From the information and feedback collected in the workshops, the Pembina Institute drafted a summary document outlining the process, the information collected from participants, and sixteen recommendations for City of Yellowknife to consider while developing their climate adaptation implementation plan.Recommendations include:Create and adopt a comprehensive adaptation policy (a template was included in the Pembina report)Hire a Climate Change Adaptation CoordinatorEstablish a multi-stakeholder Climate Change Adaptation CommitteeRequire that the Climate Adaptation Committee and Coordinator use decision support tools created by the project to create a library of resources for communityConduct outreach to public about project, tools, and informationRequire that all decisions considered in the front of the city council include a section on the &lsquo;Implications for Climate Change Adaptation&rsquo;Have goods and services suppliers provide evidence they consider climate changeEducate city&rsquo;s goods and services suppliers&nbsp; on climate change adaptationAddress all critical climate impact risksReview public infrastructure investment plans through adaptation &lsquo;lens&rsquo;Establish a schedule for review of all city&rsquo;s bylaws, polices, and plans to include adaptationCreate a line item for adaptation&nbsp; in city&rsquo;s budgetHost quarterly meetings with Committee to review all adaptation decisions madeConsider commissioning further studies of climate impacts that has greater resolution than data used in this projectCoordinate with other government bodies on adaptation effortsEncourage development of institutional support for ongoing adaptation workRecommendations developed by the project may make Yellowknife more resilient to climate impacts by incorporating future conditions into infrastructure planning and development and increasing capacity of staff and the public. While the city has begun implementing mitigation measures, the adaptation plan has not yet been released.
field_proj_status: Information collected from online resources. Updated 12/21/10
field_proj_summary: With a grant from the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs the City of Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories, Canada, engaged a group of stakeholders in an extensive adaptation planning process. The city, with the support of the Pembina Institute, hosted three workshops to discuss impacts to the region and viable local adaptation options. The project results were written up in a summary document authored by the Pembina Institute and included recommendations for the city to take to make Yellowknife more resilient to climate change.
